blocks.text: 1. ANN

blocks.alt: Slow exact search becomes ANN, producing fast, nearly-correct results

blocks.text: ANN, the general approach behind approximate nearest neighbor search, introduces the umbrella concept every remaining algorithm in this module falls under.
It accepts a small chance of missing the true nearest neighbor in exchange for much faster search, the core idea that makes vector search feasible at scale.
2. The Exact Cost Recap
Exact KNN still touches every stored vector, no matter how the comparison is optimized.
At real world scale, that linear cost becomes the actual bottleneck.
3. The Approximation Tradeoff
ANN gives up a guarantee of perfect accuracy for dramatic speed gains, the same approximate-versus-exact tradeoff introduced in What is a Vector Database.
It accepts a small, usually negligible, chance of missing the true best match in exchange for searching far fewer vectors.

blocks.text: 4. Recall As The Correctness Measure

blocks.alt: True nearest neighbors are compared for recall against found neighbors

blocks.text: Recall measures how often ANN finds the true nearest neighbors that exact search would have found, using the same precision and recall concepts covered in Embedding Evaluation.
A recall close to one hundred percent means ANN is rarely missing anything important.
5. The Family Of ANN Algorithms

blocks.alt: HNSW, IVF, and LSH form a family of ANN algorithms

blocks.text: HNSW, IVF, LSH, and several others all pursue the same underlying goal through different techniques.
Each gets its own dedicated topic later in this module.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Every algorithm covered for the rest of this module represents a different strategy for achieving the same fundamental ANN tradeoff introduced here, trading a small accuracy loss for dramatically faster search.

blocks.text: 6. Narrowing Candidates Before Comparing

blocks.alt: All vectors narrow to a candidate set, then a final comparison

blocks.text: Most ANN algorithms narrow down candidates before computing exact distances, building on the same idea behind what an index does, as covered in Indexing.
Only a small subset of vectors ever gets a full distance calculation.
7. Tuning Accuracy Versus Speed

blocks.alt: High accuracy is compared against high speed

blocks.text: Nearly every ANN algorithm exposes a knob controlling how thoroughly it searches, similar to the index parameter tuning covered in Indexing.
Turning that knob trades recall against raw query speed.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Increasing an ANN algorithm's search thoroughness setting improves recall by checking more candidates, but also increases query latency, the same fundamental tradeoff explored across every algorithm in this module.

blocks.text: 8. When Approximation Is Acceptable
A RAG system rarely needs the single mathematically perfect match, echoing the retrieval precision discussion in Why Chunking.
A very good, very fast match usually serves the downstream model just as well.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When ANN Is The Right Choice Over Exact Search

blocks.alt: A large-scale dataset points toward using ANN

blocks.text: Large collections needing fast query latency need ANN.
Small collections needing perfect accuracy can stick with exact brute force or KNN search instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below measures recall by comparing an approximate search shortcut against exact results.

code.content:
import random

def euclidean_distance(v1, v2):
    return sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) ** 0.5

def exact_knn(query, vectors, k):
    distances = [(i, euclidean_distance(query, v)) for i, v in enumerate(vectors)]
    distances.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
    return set(i for i, _ in distances[:k])

def approximate_search(query, vectors, k, sample_fraction=0.3):
    # only compare against a random sample instead of every vector
    sample_size = int(len(vectors) * sample_fraction)
    sample_indices = random.sample(range(len(vectors)), sample_size)
    distances = [(i, euclidean_distance(query, vectors[i])) for i in sample_indices]
    distances.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
    return set(i for i, _ in distances[:k])

vectors = [[random.random() for _ in range(16)] for _ in range(2000)]
query = [random.random() for _ in range(16)]

k = 10
exact_results = exact_knn(query, vectors, k)
approx_results = approximate_search(query, vectors, k)

overlap = len(exact_results & approx_results)
recall = overlap / k

print(f"Exact KNN checked all {len(vectors)} vectors")
print(f"Approximate search checked only {int(len(vectors) * 0.3)} vectors")
print(f"Recall: {recall:.2f}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the approximate search finding most, though not necessarily all, of the same neighbors exact search found while checking far fewer vectors, exactly the approximation tradeoff ANN makes.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming ANN always returns the mathematically perfect nearest neighbors like exact search does.
Never measuring recall to confirm an ANN configuration is actually acceptable for a use case.
Using exact search on a very large collection when ANN would offer far better latency.
Tuning an ANN algorithm's accuracy versus speed knob without testing the actual impact on results.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: ANN accepts a small chance of missing the true nearest neighbor for much faster search.
Exact KNN still touches every stored vector, becoming a bottleneck at real world scale.
ANN trades a guarantee of perfect accuracy for dramatic speed gains.
Recall measures how often ANN finds the true nearest neighbors exact search would have found.
HNSW, IVF, LSH, and other algorithms all pursue the same ANN goal through different techniques.
Most ANN algorithms narrow down candidates before computing exact distances on a small subset.
Nearly every ANN algorithm exposes a tunable knob trading recall against raw query speed.
A RAG system rarely needs the single perfect match; a very good, fast match usually suffices.
